results.input: Studies 101–120: foundational muscle architecture and measurement methods

output.group: 101–120 — Foundational muscle architecture and measurement methods
output.measurement_and_model_limits: The foundational cadaver datasets are not interchangeable with living, contracting muscle. Ward et al. explicitly note the small and poorly characterized older reference datasets, while Kawakami et al. showed with ultrasound that fascicle behavior during passive motion and active contraction differs materially; therefore resting cadaver values should not be treated as subject-specific dynamic inputs [2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18972175/) [6](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9109557/). Narici’s review correctly describes ultrasound and MRI as non-invasive in-vivo approaches, but the record also emphasizes that architecture varies with contraction and that preservation and age can bias cadaver measurements [7](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10098710/). Charles et al. (PMID 31613899) is a living-adult lower-limb DTI dataset, but DTI tractography is an imaging-derived estimate rather than direct dissection; it should not be silently merged with cadaver architecture tables [8](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31613899/). The 2022 “From fibre to function” review (PMID 35388613) is correctly used for uncertainty caused by sparse fiber sampling and simplified architecture-to-performance extrapolation [9](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35388613/). Lee et al. (PMID 22406468) concerns robust PCSA estimation and geometric reconstruction, including improved robustness in synthetic-data comparisons, not a universal validation of PCSA in every muscle or population [10](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22406468/). Kwah et al. (PMID 23305989), Van Hooren et al. (PMID 32163334), and the panoramic-ultrasound review (PMID 33189413) are measurement-method reviews; reliability and validity depend on muscle, operator, probe field, posture, contraction state, fascicle visibility, and protocol [11](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23305989/) [12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32163334/) [13](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33189413/). DTI reviews (PMIDs 26236177 and 27257975) support three-dimensional fiber-orientation assessment but identify acquisition, resolution, tractography, and interpretation constraints [14](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26236177/) [15](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27257975/). Balshaw et al. (PMID 33935234) studied 52 recreationally active men and found that volume was at least as strongly associated with quadriceps strength as effective PCSA or maximum ACSA; this is a population- and task-specific association, not a general force law [16](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33935234/). Maganaris et al. (PMID 15972215) studied 21 healthy men and found no significant relation between measured fiber length and tendon moment arm across the sampled muscles; individual L/d ratios therefore should not be inferred from skeletal size alone [17](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15972215/). The packet’s 2017 mechanics/energetics/plasticity citation (PMID 29058612) is a conference-session summary/review, useful for conceptual coverage of sarcomere length, passive and series elasticity, 3-D deformation, modeling, and clinical muscle properties, but not a primary validation dataset [18](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29058612/).
output.safe_model_implications: An anatomy or exercise-mechanics model may disclose architecture as a **capacity-related descriptor**, using fiber/fascicle length, pennation, volume, ACSA/PCSA, and moment arm as distinct variables with explicit source, population, posture, contraction state, and measurement modality. It may explain the general direction that more fibers in parallel support force capacity and more sarcomeres in series support excursion/shortening capacity, while labeling this as a model framework rather than an individual force estimate [1](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/6617027/) [5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3130443/). It should preserve provenance and uncertainty rather than collapse cadaver, ultrasound, MRI, and DTI values into one canonical number; dynamic disclosures should state that fascicle, tendon, and joint motion can be mechanically decoupled [6](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9109557/) [7](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10098710/). It may compare muscles or explain why regional and subject-specific architecture matters, but it should not produce unvalidated individual force values, injury predictions, clinical decisions, or exercise prescriptions from these studies alone. For model confidence, report ranges or qualitative confidence labels, expose measurement location and protocol, and require independent moment-arm, activation, external-load, and subject-specific validation before translating architecture into joint torque or muscle-force claims [9](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35388613/) [16](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33935234/) [17](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15972215/).
output.verified_findings: The packet’s core citations are substantially verified. Wickiewicz et al. (PMID 6617027) is a cadaveric lower-limb architecture study of knee extensors/flexors and ankle plantar-/dorsiflexors; it reported fiber-length and pennation patterns and linked sarcomeres in parallel with tension potential and sarcomeres in series with shortening-velocity potential [1](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/6617027/). Ward et al. (PMID 18972175) is the 27-muscle, 21-lower-extremity cadaver dataset; it measured fiber length and PCSA and explicitly framed them as determinants of excursion and force-generating capacity, while challenging the assumption that two-joint muscles necessarily have longer fibers [2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18972175/). Lieber and Fridén’s 2000 and 2001 reviews (PMIDs 11054744 and 11210948) correctly cover whole-muscle architecture, force/excursion capacity, motor-unit arrangement, adaptation, and surgical relevance [3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11054744/) [4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11210948/). Lieber and Ward (PMID 21502118) is correctly identified as a framework review connecting fiber length and PCSA with excursion, shortening velocity, and force [5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3130443/).

results.input: Studies 121–140: muscle moment arms, leverage, and elbow/knee/ankle force-estimation context

output.measurement_and_model_limits:
These sources do not establish universal muscle forces, individual PCSA values, injury risk, or exercise prescriptions. The evidence is heterogeneous: passive MRI, cadaveric three-dimensional kinematics, biplane X-ray during selected tasks, ultrasound excursion, anatomical specimens, and computational models are not interchangeable measurement regimes. Moment arm depends on joint angle, reference axis, tendon load, contraction state, forearm orientation, and the method used to estimate it. In particular, tendon-excursion calculations can be coordinate-dependent [1](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23998280/) and can differ substantially from MRI center-of-rotation estimates [6](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20847130/).

Generalization is constrained by small and selected samples: the cited knee MRI study included 17 adults, the ankle MRI study ten men, the Achilles comparison nine participants, the elbow in-vivo contraction study ten young men, and the functional knee study ten healthy young people. Cadaver results cannot be assumed to reproduce living, loaded, actively contracting behavior. A joint torque divided by a moment arm is not, by itself, a unique muscle-force solution: multiple muscles, antagonists, co-contraction, changing lines of action, tendon compliance, passive tissues, and optimization assumptions affect force sharing. The packet’s percentage attribution in Study 139 should therefore be treated as a study-specific modeled result, not a general anatomical constant.
output.safe_model_implications:
An anatomy or exercise-mechanics information model may safely represent moment arms as **joint-, posture-, method-, load-, and subject-dependent parameters**, with provenance fields for source, modality, reference axis, contraction state, and uncertainty. It should distinguish geometric/effective moment arm from tendon-excursion estimates and should never silently substitute one for the other.

For disclosures, the model may explain the directional mechanics supported here: changing posture changes leverage; patellar-tendon leverage is governed by three-dimensional knee geometry and instantaneous-axis definition; Achilles and tibialis-anterior leverage vary across ankle range; and elbow-flexor leverage depends on elbow angle, forearm orientation, and contraction state. It may report study-population ranges or qualitative trends only when clearly labeled, while avoiding individualized force estimates, claims that one muscle must carry a fixed percentage of torque, injury predictions, or training prescriptions. Any force-estimation output should be presented as a conditional model scenario with explicit assumptions and sensitivity to moment-arm method, muscle recruitment, and subject geometry.
output.verified_findings:
The packet’s core citation, **“Muscle moment-arms: a key element in muscle-force estimation” (PMID 23998280)**, is verified as a mechanics/modeling paper. It defines moment arms using rigid-body joint mechanics and screw theory, and warns that an improperly applied tendon-excursion method can produce relative force-solution errors from 0% to 100% in its conceptual example [1](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23998280/). **Study 122 (PMID 11415658)** is verified as an in-vivo MRI study of seven knee muscles plus the patellar tendon in 17 adults; passive sagittal and frontal-plane moment arms changed with knee angle, and many measures differed by sex, supporting angle- and sex-specific inputs rather than a single generic value [2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11415658/). **Study 123 (PMID 15047009)** is verified as a three-dimensional fresh-cadaver study of the patellar-tendon moment arm. Its effective moment arm was defined relative to the tibiofemoral screw axis; peak values in six knees were 4–6 cm near 45° flexion, with departures from the simple perpendicular-distance interpretation near full extension [3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15047009/). **Study 125 (PMID 34062347)** is verified as a biplane-X-ray in-vivo study in ten healthy young participants performing six activities. Mean patellar-tendon moment arm was approximately 46 mm through 0–70° flexion and varied more between people than between activities, emphasizing subject-specific joint geometry [4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34062347/).

**Study 127 (PMID 2373722)** is verified as an MRI study of Achilles-tendon and tibialis-anterior moment arms in ten adult men. Across maximal dorsiflexion to plantarflexion, Achilles moment arms increased by about 20% while tibialis-anterior moment arms decreased by about 30%; fixed- versus moving-center calculations differed only modestly in that study [5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2373722/). **Study 128 (PMID 20847130)** is verified as a comparison of MRI center-of-rotation and ultrasound tendon-excursion methods in nine participants. The methods correlated strongly but differed by approximately 25–30% in absolute Achilles moment-arm magnitude, demonstrating that method choice can materially alter model inputs [6](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20847130/). **Study 134 (PMID 7775488)** is verified as anatomical measurement plus computer modeling of elbow muscles. Flexion/extension moment arms changed by at least 30% over a 95° range; biceps flexion leverage peaked in a more extended elbow and was larger with supination, while supination leverage changed with elbow extension [7](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7775488/). **Study 135 (PMID 22431216)** is verified as an MRI study of biceps brachii, brachialis, and brachioradialis in ten young men at rest and during 20% and 60% isometric contractions. Moment arms generally increased during contraction, plausibly from contraction-induced muscle thickening, with effects varying by muscle and joint position [8](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22431216/). The remaining packet entries—Studies 124, 126, 129–133, and 136–140—are appropriately classified by their supplied titles as patellar/Achilles moment-arm measurement, elbow moment-arm scaling/anatomy, and elbow functional-capacity or load-sharing modeling studies; their supplied PMID identifiers should be retained as lookup keys, but no additional numerical claim is made here without direct record-level verification.

results.input: Studies 141–155: shoulder, chest, deltoid, rotator-cuff, and upper-limb mechanics

output.group: 141–155 — Shoulder / chest / deltoid / rotator cuff mechanics
output.measurement_and_model_limits:
Moment arm is leverage—perpendicular distance or the local tendon-excursion derivative—not muscle force, activation, joint contact force, injury risk, or training effect [1] [2]. Values vary with humeral elevation plane, axial position, joint translation, scapular posture, line-of-action definition, and whether the geometric or tendon-excursion method is used. The systematic review specifically notes uncertainty in locating the glenohumeral center and in representing joint translation and broad attachment regions [1].

Studies 142–146 are primarily cadaveric or in-vitro and therefore do not directly establish living-subject activation, fatigue, tendon compliance, reflex control, or task-specific loading. Study 142 used eight elderly cadaveric upper extremities, even though degenerative shoulders were excluded; this limits direct transfer to young, injured, trained, or otherwise different populations [2]. Study 143–146 results are configuration-specific and should not be generalized to every exercise, grip, load, or scapulothoracic strategy [3] [4] [5] [6].

Study 147 used MRI geometry from one healthy 26-year-old male and approximated fiber maps and constitutive properties in a finite-element model; it demonstrates a modeling phenomenon, not universal individual fiber mechanics or validated force estimates [7]. Studies 148–150 and 153–155 are model-dependent: predicted forces/load sharing depend on geometry, degrees of freedom, muscle-tendon parameters, objective functions, kinematic inputs, stability constraints, and calibration. Study 154 concerns altered arthroplasty geometry and cannot be transferred to an intact shoulder. Study 155 concerns sensor and model agreement, not proof that modeled muscle or joint loads are clinically exact [8] [9] [10] [11] [12] [13].

No citation in this section justifies invented individual force values, architecture values, injury probabilities, or exercise prescriptions. Studies 151 and 152 remain unverified until complete bibliographic identifiers are supplied.
output.safe_model_implications:
Represent shoulder muscles as **configuration-dependent torque-capacity contributors**, with signed moment arms indexed by joint position and movement plane. Do not map a large moment arm directly to a unique prime-mover label or to a predicted force; expose the distinction between leverage, activation, force-generating capacity, and joint-stability contribution [1] [2].

For broad or multipennate muscles, use regional compartments where the evidence supports them—such as anterior/middle/posterior deltoid and selected pectoralis, latissimus, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and subscapularis regions—rather than assuming one uniform line of action [2] [7]. Allow within-muscle fibers or compartments to have different, even opposing, rotational actions when using a high-fidelity model, but label such outputs as model-dependent [7].

Include antagonist/co-contraction and stability as possible contributors, and state the optimization assumptions whenever muscle-sharing results are displayed [8]. Treat upper-limb and surgical-transfer models as geometry- and scenario-specific reference models, not as clinical predictions [9] [10] [11] [12]. For IMU-driven loading, disclose sensor placement, kinematic uncertainty, model constraints, and validation scope [13]. The information model should therefore return source, study class, specimen/population, tested configuration, measurement method, uncertainty/transfer boundary, and an explicit “not a force/injury/prescription estimate” guardrail.
output.verified_findings:
The packet’s core citations are bibliographically supported. Study 141, Hik & Ackland, “The moment arms of the muscles spanning the glenohumeral joint: a systematic review” (J Anat 2019; PMID 30411350; DOI 10.1111/joa.12903), is a systematic review of deltoid, pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, teres major, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, subscapularis, and teres minor moment arms during abduction, flexion, and axial rotation [1]. It reports the anterior/middle deltoid as substantial elevators, pectoralis major/latissimus dorsi/teres major as prominent depressor-adductors, and the cuff as the principal axial-rotation group; these are leverage findings, not direct muscle-force measurements [1].

Study 142, Ackland et al., “Moment arms of the muscles crossing the anatomical shoulder” (J Anat 2008; PMID 18691376; DOI 10.1111/j.1469-7580.2008.00965.x), is an eight-cadaver tendon-excursion study of 18 muscle sub-regions. It supports meaningful regional differences: anterior and middle deltoid were effective abductors; selected teres-major, latissimus, and pectoralis-major regions were effective adductors; clavicular pectoralis-major and anterior deltoid/supraspinatus regions contributed to flexion, while teres major and posterior deltoid had larger extension leverage [2].

Study 143, Kuechle et al., “Shoulder muscle moment arms during horizontal flexion and elevation” (J Shoulder Elbow Surg 1997; PMID 9356931), is a tendon-excursion moment-arm study of 10 shoulder muscles. The source record supports plane- and position-dependent leverage: deltoid had the largest elevation moment arm, pectoralis major the largest horizontal-flexion moment arm at 90° elevation, and pectoralis major/latissimus/teres major prominent depressor or adductor leverage [3]. Study 144, Ackland et al., “Moment arms of the shoulder muscles during axial rotation” (PMID 21064160), and study 145, Kuechle et al., “The relevance of the moment arm of shoulder muscles with respect to axial rotation of the glenohumeral joint in four positions” (PMID 10758292), are directly relevant axial-rotation moment-arm studies; their study class is cadaveric/in-vitro tendon-excursion or geometric shoulder biomechanics, rather than in-vivo force validation [4] [5].

Study 146, Hoffmann et al., “Moment arms of the deltoid, infraspinatus and teres minor muscles for movements with high range of motion: A cadaveric study” (PMID 35671631), is a cadaveric high-ROM moment-arm study and supports position-dependent changes in deltoid and cuff leverage, with infraspinatus and teres minor providing substantial external-rotation leverage in the tested configurations [6]. Study 147 is correctly identified by DOI 10.1080/10255842.2012.719605 as Webb, Blemker & Delp, “3D Finite Element Models of Shoulder Muscles for Computing Lines of Actions and Moment Arms” (PMID 22994141). It is a subject-specific computational finite-element study showing that fiber-level moment arms can vary substantially within a muscle; its supraspinatus example demonstrates that different fiber regions can have opposing rotational actions [7].

Study 148, “Static optimization underestimates antagonist muscle activity at the glenohumeral joint: A musculoskeletal modeling study” (PMID 31668905), is a computational/EMG-informed modeling study. It supports the modeling caution that antagonist activity may contribute to glenohumeral stability and can be underestimated by conventional static optimization [8]. Study 149, Holzbaur et al., “A model of the upper extremity for simulating musculoskeletal surgery and analyzing neuromuscular control” (J Biomech 2005; PMID 16078622), is a multi-degree-of-freedom upper-extremity musculoskeletal model spanning shoulder, elbow, forearm, wrist, thumb, and index finger [9]. Study 150, Garner & Pandy, “Musculoskeletal model of the upper limb based on the Visible Human Male dataset” (PMID 11264863), is an image-derived mathematical upper-limb model, useful as a geometry/modeling reference rather than a population-norm force study [10].

The packet’s study 151 title, “Biomechanical couplings between elbow and forearm movements,” and study 152 title, “The influence of task and angle on torque production and muscle activity at the elbow,” are plausible upper-limb mechanics topics, but the supplied packet gives no authors, journal, DOI, or PMID for either; they cannot be uniquely verified from the packet alone and should be marked bibliographically incomplete pending a full reference. Study 153 is verified as Kontaxis et al., “Biomechanical analysis of latissimus dorsi, pectoralis major, and pectoralis minor transfers in subscapularis-deficient shoulders” (2022; PMID 34592410), a computational surgical-transfer study comparing altered lines of action and biomechanical properties under subscapularis-deficient conditions [11]. Study 154, “Moment arms of the shoulder musculature after reverse total shoulder arthroplasty” (PMID 20439669), is a clinical computational/cadaveric arthroplasty biomechanics study; the record supports increased moment arms of major shoulder abductors, flexors, adductors, and extensors after the modeled reverse arthroplasty geometry [12]. Study 155, Fang et al., “On the use of inertial measurement units and musculoskeletal modeling in the calculation of muscle and joint loading at the shoulder” (PMID 40701751), is a recent measurement-validation/modeling study comparing IMU-derived upper-limb kinematics with optical motion analysis and evaluating effects on estimated shoulder muscle and joint loading [13].

results.input: Studies 156–170: hamstring, quadriceps, and regional muscle architecture

output.measurement_and_model_limits:
The evidence mixes cadaveric anatomy, static ultrasound, MRI/DTI, training interventions, healthy-aging cohorts, sprint simulations, and theoretical or animal-based models. Cadaveric measurements in study 157 came from older specimens and cannot be treated as direct measurements of living athletic populations. Study 161 describes young athletes rather than the general population. Studies 158–159 estimate musculotendon lengths, forces, stretch, and work through scaled or forward-dynamic models; they do not directly measure internal fiber force or establish individual injury risk. Their treadmill speeds, participant samples, EMG constraints, model scaling, assumed moment arms, and muscle-tendon parameters limit transfer to other tasks and people.

Ultrasound pennation and fascicle-length estimates are site-, probe-, posture-, contraction-, and operator-dependent; superficial visualized fascicles do not necessarily represent the whole muscle. MRI and DTI provide geometry or diffusion-derived proxies with acquisition, segmentation, tractography, and biological-interpretation limits; DTI measures should not be equated automatically with histological fascicle length or contractile force. Specific tension and PCSA-based inference depends on tendon-force estimation, pennation correction, activation, moment arms, and measurement location, so it cannot yield a universal force-per-area constant from these citations alone.

Study 164 is a particular training protocol and sample, not a general rule that all eccentric work lengthens fascicles or all concentric work increases pennation. Study 165–166 findings are age- and cohort-dependent associations, not individual diagnoses or inevitable trajectories. Study 167 addresses group-level size-strength relationships; it does not validate force prediction for a particular person or exercise. Studies 168–170 demonstrate consequences of geometry and modeling assumptions, but study 168 is a geometric/modeling analysis and study 169 uses rabbit tissue geometry, so neither directly supplies human regional force values. No cited study supports individual injury prediction, a guaranteed exercise effect, or a precise prescription.
output.safe_model_implications:
An anatomy or exercise-mechanics information model should represent BFlh, BFsh, semitendinosus, and semimembranosus as distinct structures, preserve proximal–distal and regional fields where available, and avoid collapsing the hamstrings into one uniform architecture [1] [2]. It should keep measured observations separate from model-derived estimates and label whether a value comes from cadaver, ultrasound, MRI/DTI, simulation, intervention, or animal work.

For sprint or joint-mechanics explanations, the model may state that biarticular-muscle moment arms, posture, running speed, and lumbo-pelvic coordination can alter estimated musculotendon length and loading, especially during late swing [3] [4]. It should not convert those findings into a personalized injury probability or claim that a single muscle is predictably injured in a given user. For quadriceps and other pennate muscles, the model may explain that PCSA, fascicle length, pennation, muscle size, tendon force, and measurement location jointly affect force inference [6] [7] [10], while presenting uncertainty rather than a single deterministic force estimate.

The model should support regional heterogeneity and geometry-aware representations: local architecture can produce different fiber strains and mechanical outputs within one muscle, and 3-D or micromechanical models may matter when internal depth, width, anisotropy, or nonuniform geometry is the question [11] [12] [13]. Simpler models remain acceptable when their stated target is narrow and their assumptions are disclosed. Aging, athletic status, training history, sex, task, and measurement method should be explicit applicability metadata, and the system should refuse to infer unprovided architecture values, individual force estimates, injury predictions, or exercise prescriptions from these studies alone.
output.verified_findings:
The packet’s citations for 156, 157, 158, 159, 160, 161, 162, 164, 166, 167, 168, 169, and 170 are bibliographically traceable in PubMed, publisher, or full-text records. Study 156 is Kellis et al.’s 2018 narrative review, which reports meaningful inter- and intra-muscular variation: the biceps femoris long head (BFlh) has relatively short, pennated fibers; semitendinosus has relatively longer fascicles and lower relative strain for a given joint motion; and proximal–distal architecture can differ within a muscle [1](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30117053/). Study 157 is Kellis et al. (2012), an eight-cadaver dissection study measuring fiber length, sarcomere length, PCSA, and pennation. It found distinct medial-versus-lateral hamstring designs and concluded that treating the hamstrings as one uniform muscle group reduces functional-model accuracy [2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22564790/).

Study 158 is Thelen et al. (2005), a 14-athlete treadmill study using 3-D kinematics and scaled musculoskeletal models. Estimated peak musculotendon lengths occurred in late swing; the BFlh estimate exceeded those of semitendinosus and semimembranosus, and modeled intermuscle moment-arm differences contributed to the variation [3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15632676/). Study 159 is Chumanov et al. (2007), involving 19 athletes, EMG, kinematics, and forward-dynamic simulation. The model found late-swing peak stretch, speed-related increases in peak hamstring force and negative work, and substantial influence of lumbo-pelvic muscles on BFlh stretch; these are modeled mechanics findings, not direct injury observations [4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17659291/). Study 160, “Spatial-frequency Analysis of the Anatomical Differences in Hamstring Muscles,” is traceable by PMID 33563139 in the packet; its citation identity is verified, but the supplied packet does not state enough detail to safely summarize its specific measurements or conclusions.

Study 161 is Tate et al. (2006), an MRI-based description of lower-extremity muscle volume and peak CSA in young athletes [5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16394964/). Study 162 is Rutherford and Jones (1992), which used real-time ultrasound to measure pennation in vastus lateralis and vastus intermedius in vivo [6](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1425649/). Study 163 is identifiable as the Maganaris et al. in-vivo specific-tension work cited in the packet, but the packet gives no PMID, DOI, or complete title; it should therefore be retained as a provisional bibliographic record until the original record is attached. Study 164 is Franchi et al. (2014), which reported different architectural responses to concentric versus eccentric resistance training, with the study’s eccentric condition showing greater fascicle-length change and the concentric condition greater pennation-angle change [7](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24387247/).

Study 165 is Narici et al. (2003), correctly identified by the supplied DOI as an aging-and-architecture study [8](https://doi.org/10.1152/japplphysiol.00433.2003). Study 166 is Cameron et al. (2023), PMID 37162031, using diffusion-tensor MRI in a healthy-aging cohort to examine age-related muscle microstructure and architecture and their association with strength [9](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37162031/). Study 167 is Balshaw et al. (2021), which examined whether architecture, calculated muscle force, and measurement location improve the muscle-size/strength relationship [10](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33935234/). Study 168 is Azizi and Deslauriers (2014), a geometric/modeling and empirical-strain analysis showing that regional architectural variation can produce heterogeneous fiber strain within a muscle, including higher modeled strain at lower pennation angles and differences between superficial and central fibers in fusiform geometry [11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4129366/). Study 169 is Sharafi and Blemker (2010), a micromechanical model based on histological cross-sections of rabbit rectus femoris and soleus; it showed that fiber/fascicle geometry materially affects predicted macroscopic shear behavior and that fascicle-level behavior can be transversely anisotropic [12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20846654/). Study 170 is Randhawa and Wakeling (2015), which compared 1-D, 2-D, and 3-D structural models during human plantarflexion. The 3-D model better represented opposing depth changes and predicted pennation more accurately in the tested setting, although with mean parameters it was not superior to a simpler 1-D model for the fascicle-length/pennation relationship [13](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26073723/).

results.input: Studies 171–185: tendon, fascicle, and muscle-tendon mechanics

output.measurement_and_model_limits:
The evidence mixes reviews, laboratory experiments, in-vivo ultrasound or imaging, developmental synthesis, spaceflight/unloading research, and computational models. Tendon and aponeurosis strain are method- and site-dependent; estimates depend on image tracking, force estimation, joint kinematics, tendon geometry, and assumptions about homogeneous or transmitted force. Muscle fascicle behavior cannot be inferred from joint angle or whole muscle–tendon length alone. The cited papers therefore support mechanism classes and conditional relationships, not a single universal fascicle velocity, tendon stiffness, force value, or muscle contribution.

Population and task transfer are bounded. Several findings concern healthy young adults, selected lower-limb muscles, specific gait or contraction conditions, children versus adults, or specialized cohorts exposed to spaceflight. A review or meta-analysis summarizes heterogeneous protocols and does not erase between-study differences in stretch dose, imaging method, muscle, training status, or follow-up. Spaceflight findings should not be treated as ordinary resistance-training effects, and developmental morphology should not be extrapolated to adults without qualification.

Hill-type and related models are useful abstractions, not direct measurements of individual fibers. Predicted force and torque can be sensitive to moment arms, fascicle lengths, tendon compliance, force–length and force–velocity parameters, activation assumptions, optimization objective, and subject-specific geometry. MRI-derived moment arms and tendon-excursion methods have measurement uncertainty, and static optimization may not reproduce antagonist coactivation or neural control. No cited item justifies individual force estimates, injury predictions, or clinical prescriptions without subject-specific measurements and validation.
output.safe_model_implications:
An anatomy or exercise-mechanics information model may represent the muscle–tendon unit as a coupled system with distinct contractile, aponeurotic, and tendon components. It should allow fascicle length and velocity to differ from whole muscle–tendon length and joint angular velocity, and it should record whether a claim comes from direct imaging, inferred tendon force, a review, or a computational model [1] [2] [12].

The model should attach provenance and uncertainty to moment arms, fascicle architecture, tendon properties, operating lengths, and predicted forces. It should preserve muscle-, region-, joint-angle-, task-, age-, training-, and population-specific qualifiers rather than collapsing results into fixed values. Duplicate study tags may point to one canonical record, while separate study classes and measurement modalities remain distinct.

Safe disclosures can state that tendon compliance can mediate force transmission and fascicle operating behavior; architecture and leverage jointly affect modeled mechanical capacity; and model outputs are conditional estimates whose confidence depends on input quality and validation [1] [5] [13] [14]. The system should explicitly label extrapolations, avoid converting cohort averages into personal prescriptions, and refrain from asserting injury risk, exact force sharing, or guaranteed adaptation from this section alone.
output.verified_findings:
The packet’s citations are bibliographically verified as follows. **171** is Fukashiro, Hay and Nagano (2006), a peer-reviewed review of muscle–tendon-complex behavior in dynamic human movement (PMID 16871004; DOI [10.1123/jab.22.2.131](https://doi.org/10.1123/jab.22.2.131)). **172** is Magnusson et al. results.input: Studies 186–200: musculoskeletal modeling and interpretation uncertainty

output.measurement_and_model_limits:
These studies do not validate a single universal human model. Delp, Holzbaur, and Visible Human are geometry-and-parameter models whose outputs depend on selected degrees of freedom, muscle compartments, wrapping surfaces, activation inputs, force–length/velocity parameters, and kinematic assumptions. Their agreement with measured joint moments or geometry is conditional validation, not proof that individual muscle forces are uniquely identified.

Arnold’s accuracy result came from three lower-extremity cadaveric specimens, specific muscles, MRI reconstructions, wrapping surfaces, and tested hip/knee ranges; it cannot be transferred unchanged to all people, joints, postures, loads, or living tissues. Kian’s antagonist finding used four healthy adults, six submaximal shoulder tasks, and a comparison of EMG-driven and static-optimization approaches; it supports model-form uncertainty, not a universal antagonist-force percentage or injury conclusion.

DTI, ultrasound, MRI, PCSA, fascicle-length, pennation, and volume estimates are modality- and protocol-dependent. Ultrasound is commonly two-dimensional and can be affected by probe placement, fascicle visibility, curvature, joint position, contraction, operator technique, and movement; DTI depends on acquisition, tractography, registration, and interpretation assumptions. A small healthy-adult sample, cadaver data, older or athletic cohorts, and a single measurement location should not be treated as interchangeable population references. Architecture variables, moment arms, EMG, and model parameters also do not by themselves establish clinical causation, injury risk, or training outcome. Study 193 lacks enough metadata for citation-level verification and should not be used as a quantitative authority until resolved.
output.safe_model_implications:
Represent muscle targeting as a conditional, uncertainty-aware inference rather than a deterministic mapping from exercise name to one muscle or one force. Expose joint posture, external moment, muscle line of action, moment arm, architecture source, activation assumption, and whether the result is measured, simulated, or inferred. Preserve regional compartments where source evidence supports them, and allow co-contraction or antagonist activity instead of assuming only the largest agonist is active.

Use subject- and task-specific model labels and report ranges, sensitivity, or qualitative confidence rather than invented individual force estimates. Separate geometry claims from activation and force claims: a reliable moment arm does not uniquely determine muscle force, and a measured fascicle length or PCSA does not independently determine exercise loading. Attach cohort, modality, posture, contraction state, and validation domain to every architecture or mechanics record; do not silently transfer cadaveric, DTI, ultrasound, or generic-model values across populations.

For user-facing disclosures, the safe statement is that architecture and leverage influence potential force, excursion, and joint torque, while actual recruitment and loading depend on posture, task demands, neural activation, passive tissues, external load, and model assumptions. Do not present these studies as prescriptions, individualized diagnoses, injury predictions, or proof that a named exercise uniquely isolates a muscle. Store overlapping citations under one paper identifier with multiple conceptual tags, as the packet itself recommends.
output.verified_findings:
The packet’s core citations are bibliographically confirmed for Delp et al. 1990 (PMID 2210784), Holzbaur et al. 2005 (PMID 16078622), Garner & Pandy’s Visible Human upper-limb model (PMID 11264863), Arnold et al. 2000 (PMID 10862133), Ingram et al. 2015 (PMID 23998280), Kian et al. 2019 (PMID 31668905), the DTI volumetric-fiber method (PMID 35085267), Lee et al. 2012 (PMID 22406468), Balshaw et al. 2021 (PMID 33935234), Kwah et al. 2013 (PMID 23305989), Van Hooren et al. 2020 (PMID 32163334), Narici et al. 2023 (PMID 37244210), Charles et al. 2019 (PMID 31613899), and Ward et al. 2009 (PMID 18972175). The packet’s citation for Study 193, “From fibre to function: are we accurately representing muscle architecture and performance?” (2022), is not uniquely identifiable from the supplied entry alone and should remain provisional until its authors, journal, DOI, or PMID are added.

Delp et al. modeled 43 lower-extremity musculotendon actuators, joint kinematics, lines of action, and isometric force–length behavior; modeled joint moments compared favorably with experimental isometric moments, and the framework supported surgical-geometry simulations [186](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2210784/). Holzbaur et al. modeled 15 upper-extremity degrees of freedom and 50 muscle compartments, estimating muscle–tendon lengths, moment arms, muscle forces, and joint moments across postures; comparisons captured important upper-extremity geometry and mechanics and demonstrated inter-joint coupling [187](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16078622/). The Visible Human model is a mathematical upper-limb model derived from high-resolution medical images [188](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11264863/).

Arnold et al. tested MRI-derived lower-extremity models against experimental cadaver measurements and reported average moment-arm errors below 4 mm and within 10% over the tested hip/knee flexion ranges [189](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10862133/). Ingram et al. formalized muscle moment arms in musculoskeletal modeling and emphasized that correct moment-arm calculation is central to optimization-based force estimation [190](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23998280/). Kian et al. found that, in four healthy adults performing submaximal shoulder tasks, EMG-driven modeling predicted antagonist activity that static optimization largely omitted; resulting glenohumeral joint-force estimates differed substantially [191](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31668905/). The DTI method paper supports volumetric estimation of fiber orientations and fiber-angle changes in leg muscles [192](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35085267/). Lee et al. proposed geometry-based reconstruction for more robust PCSA estimation [194](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22406468/). Balshaw et al. directly evaluated muscle-size indices, architecture, force, and measurement location rather than treating size alone as a universal strength proxy [195](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33935234/). The ultrasound and imaging reviews support architecture measurement but emphasize methodological, reliability, validity, motion, and interpretation challenges [196](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32163334/) [197](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23305989/) [198](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37244210/). Charles et al. supplied a DTI-based in-vivo architecture dataset for 20 lower-limb muscles from 10 healthy adults, including fiber lengths [199](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6793854/). Ward et al. provided high-resolution lower-extremity architecture data intended to improve model accuracy and challenge existing assumptions [200](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18972175/).
